questions.prompt: Which success criterion is the most useful for reviewing AI-drafted meeting summaries?

options.text: The summary should be good, clear and useful for everyone who reads it in the team.
options.explanation: "Good", "clear" and "useful" are not specific or measurable. Two reviewers will read them differently.

options.text: Lists every decision with its owner, adds nothing new, and stays under 200 words.
options.explanation: Right. It is specific and measurable, as Anthropic's guide asks.

options.text: The team should feel happy and confident about the summary when they read it at the end.
options.explanation: A feeling is hard to check. OpenAI's guide warns against reviews based only on whether it seems to work.

questions.prompt: OpenAI's guide names two biases of a model used as a reviewer. Which are they?

options.explanation: Right. It may prefer an answer because of its place in the order, or because it is longer.
These are not the biases the guide names.

options.text: It always scores its own vendor's answers higher.
options.explanation: The guide does not say that. It names position bias and verbosity bias.

questions.prompt: When can you trust a model reviewer enough to scale it up?

options.text: Right away, because models are faster and cheaper than people, so errors are cheap.
options.explanation: Speed is not accuracy. First check that it agrees with people.

options.text: When its grades consistently agree with the grades people give the same outputs.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide says to scale up once it consistently agrees with human grades. Anthropic's guide says to test reliability first, then scale.

options.text: Never. Only people should ever review AI output at work, whatever the volume.
options.explanation: Both guides describe model reviewers as a useful, scalable option, once tested.
